label: thm:equality-case
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:equality-case}
		Let $K \in \mathcal{K}^3$. If
		\[
		V_3(\Pi K)=18V_3(K)^2,
		\]
		then $K$ is a tetrahedron.

label: prop:polytope-b-equality
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K\in \mathcal{K}^3$. In $\mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{R}^3$, we write
		\[
		\begin{gathered}
		D =\{(x,x,x):x\in K\},\\
		J_0=K\times\{0\}\times\{0\},\\
		J_1=\{0\}\times K\times\{0\},\\
		J_2=\{0\}\times\{0\}\times K,\\
	Q=J_0+J_1+J_2=K\times K\times K,
		\end{gathered}
		\]
where the addition is Minkowski addition. Define
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
		M&=V_9( D[3],J_0[2],J_1[2],J_2[2]),\\
		N&=V_9( Q[3],J_0[2],J_1[2],J_2[2]).
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		
		The calculation leading to equations~(5.7) and (5.8) in \cite {ChenFengLiXiXu2026} and the derivation of (5.9) in \cite {ChenFengLiXiXu2026} therein yield
		\[
		M=\frac{vb}{7560},\qquad M\leq N,\qquad N=\frac{v^3}{280}.
		\]
	Therefore,
		\[
		27v^2-b=\frac{7560}{v}(N-M).
		\]
		Thus
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:b-MN-equality}
			b=27v^2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M=N.
		\end{equation}
	Consider the ordered nine-tuples
		\[
		\begin{split}
			\mathscr P=( D, D, D,
			J_0,J_0,J_1,J_1,J_2,J_2),\ \ \ \ 
			\mathscr Q=(Q, Q,Q,
			J_0,J_0,J_1,J_1,J_2,J_2).
		\end{split}
		\]
		Let $u=(u_0,u_1,u_2)\in(\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{R}^3)\setminus\{0\}$. Define
		\[
		F_i:=F(K,u_i)=\{x\in K:\langle x,u_i\rangle=h_K(u_i)\},
		\qquad F(K,0):=K.
		\]
		Then
		\[
	 Q^u:=F(Q, u)=F_0\times F_1\times F_2,
		\]
		and 
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-face-intersection}
			D\cap Q^u\neq\varnothing
			\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
			F_0\cap F_1\cap F_2\neq\varnothing.
		\end{equation}
		
	Let
		$(P_i)_{i=1}^9$ and $(Q_i)_{i=1}^9$ be the members of $\mathscr P$ and
		$\mathscr Q$, respectively, and define
		$T_u=\{i:P_i\cap Q_i^u\neq\varnothing\}$. The strict-monotonicity criterion of Bihan and Soprunov
		\cite[Theorem~3.3]{BihanSoprunov2019} implies that $M<N$ if and only if, for some $u\neq 0$, the collection
		\[
		\{Q_i^u:i\in T_u\}\cup\{Q_i:i\notin T_u\}
		\]
		is essential. 
		
		If
		\eqref{eq:triple-face-intersection} holds, every member of $\mathscr P$
		touches the exposed face of the corresponding member of $\mathscr Q$.
		The nine exposed faces lie in translates of the common hyperplane $u^\perp$,
		Therefore, $\{Q_i^u:1\leq i\leq9\}$ is not essential. If
		\eqref{eq:triple-face-intersection} fails, the multiset tested by the
		criterion is
		\[
		\{Q, Q, Q,
		\iota_0F_0,\iota_0F_0,
		\iota_1F_1,\iota_1F_1,
		\iota_2F_2,\iota_2F_2\},
		\]
		where $\iota_i$ embeds $\mathbb{R}^3$ into the $i$th coordinate subspace of
		 $\mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{R}^3\times \mathbb{R}^3$.  Any subcollection containing a copy of $Q$ has
		nine-dimensional Minkowski sum. For a subcollection containing no copy of $Q$, all its members lie in the three coordinate subspaces, which form a direct sum. Examining the two repeated copies in each coordinate shows that the displayed multiset is essential if and only if
		\[
		\dim F_i\geq2\qquad(i=0,1,2).
		\]
		Thus, the inequality \(M\leq N\) is strict precisely when there exist \(F_0,F_1,F_2\), each of which is either a facet of \(K\) or \(K\) itself, such that
		\[
		F_0\cap F_1\cap F_2=\varnothing,
		\]
		where repetitions among the facets are allowed. If one
		\(F_i\) equals \(K\), then the other two facets must be disjoint.
		If two of the \(F_i\) coincide, then the repeated facet must be
		disjoint from the remaining one. In either case, replacing the
		occurrence of \(K\), or one of the repeated copies, by another
		facet yields three distinct facets with empty intersection.
		Conversely, if three distinct facets of \(K\) have empty intersection, then choosing an outer normal for each of them yields the strict inequality \(M<N\). Therefore,
		\[
		M=N
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\text{every three distinct facets of \(K\) have a common point}.
		\]
		In view of \eqref{eq:b-MN-equality}, this proves \eqref{eq:b-facet-condition}.
			
		To prove the final assertion of the proposition, it remains to show
		that every three-dimensional polytope satisfying this condition is
		a tetrahedron.  Translate \(K\) so that \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\), and let $L=K^\circ$. Under polarity, the facets of \(K\) correspond to the vertices of \(L\), and condition \eqref{eq:b-facet-condition} becomes the assertion that every three vertices of \(L\) lie in a common proper face. Fix a facet \(G\) of \(L\) and choose a vertex \(z\notin G\). For any two distinct vertices \(x,y\) of \(G\), the preceding property yields a proper face \(H\) of \(L\) containing \(x,y,z\). Since \(z\notin G\), whereas \(x,y\in G\), the three vertices \(x,y,z\) are not collinear. Consequently, \(H\) is two-dimensional and hence is a facet of \(L\). Moreover, \(H\neq G\), and \(H\cap G\) is a face containing both \(x\) and \(y\). Since two distinct facets of a three-dimensional polytope intersect in at most an edge, \(H\cap G\) must be an edge. Thus \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent. It follows that every pair of vertices of \(G\) is adjacent, forcing \(G\) to be a triangle. Since \(G\) was arbitrary, \(L\) is simplicial. Finally, every triple of vertices of \(L\) lies in a proper face, which, by simpliciality, must be the triangular facet spanned by those three vertices. Hence, every triple of vertices of \(L\) forms a facet.
		
		Let \(m=f_0(L)\) denote the number of vertices of \(L\). Since every triple of vertices of \(L\) forms a triangular facet, we have
		\[
		f_2(L)=\binom{m}{3}.
		\]
		Since \(L\) is a simplicial, each facet has three edges, and each edge belongs to exactly two facets. 
		Counting the edge-facet incidences yields
		\[
		3f_2(L)=2f_1(L).
		\]
		Combining this identity with Euler's relation
		\[
		f_0(L)-f_1(L)+f_2(L)=2
		\]
		and using \(f_0(L)=m\), we obtain
		\[
		f_2(L)=2m-4.
		\]
		Consequently,
		\[
		\binom{m}{3}=2m-4.
		\]
		Since every three-dimensional polytope has at least four vertices, we have \(m\geq4\). Hence
		\[
		\frac{m(m-1)(m-2)}{6}=2(m-2),
		\]
		and division by \(m-2>0\) yields
		\[
		m(m-1)=12.
		\]
		Thus \(m=4\). This implies that \(L\) is a tetrahedron. Since the polar of a tetrahedron is again a tetrahedron, \(K\) is also a tetrahedron. The final assertion now follows from \eqref{eq:both-equalities}.

label: prop:c-equality-facial
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that \(c=9v^2\), and let \(x,y\in\operatorname{ext}L\). If \(x\) and \(y\) lie in no common proper exposed face, then
		\[
		(x,y)\subset\operatorname{int}L.
		\]
		
		
		
		Suppose first that $x$ and $y$ are linearly independent. Take
		$P=\operatorname{span}\{x,y\}$ and $W=L\cap P$. Then every \(z\in P\) can be written uniquely as \(z=\alpha x+\beta y\). Since \(x\) and \(y\) are extreme points of \(L\), the affine line \(\{\alpha+\beta=1\}\) intersects \(W\) precisely in the segment \([x,y]\). That is,
		\[
		W\cap\{\alpha+\beta=1\}=[x,y].
		\]
		Since $(x,y)\subset\operatorname{relint} W$, $W$ has points in
		$\{\alpha+\beta>1\}$.  Choose an extreme point $z$ of the exposed face of
		$W$ on which $\alpha+\beta$ is maximal. Then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:z-coordinates}
			z=\alpha x+\beta y,\qquad
			\alpha>0,\quad\beta>0,\quad\alpha+\beta>1.
		\end{equation}
		
		
		The point $z$ lies on $\partial L$.  Let $F$ be the unique minimal face of
		$L$ whose relative interior contains $z$.  Since $z$ is extreme in the
		planar section $W$, we must have $\dim F\leq1$.  If $F$ is a segment, its linear
		span cannot equal $P$.  Moreover, since \(0\in\operatorname{int}L\) the convex cone generated by \(F\) is pointed. Hence,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:touching-polar-duality}
			\tau(x)=\mathbb{R}_+x,\qquad \tau(y)=\mathbb{R}_+y,\qquad
			\tau(z)=\operatorname{pos} F,\qquad \operatorname{pos} F\cap P=\mathbb{R}_+z.
		\end{equation}
		Here, we use the duality between faces of $L=K^\circ$ and touching cones of
		$K$.
		
		Let
		\[
		\widetilde w=(\alpha x,\beta y)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		w=\frac{\widetilde w}{\|\widetilde w\|}\in\mathbb S^5.
		\]
		Equations \eqref{eq:touching-product-diagonal},
		\eqref{eq:z-coordinates}, and \eqref{eq:touching-polar-duality} give
		\[
		\begin{split}
			\dim T(Q,w)=2, \ \ 
			\dim T(C,w)=3+\dim\tau(z)\leq5, \ \
			\dim\bigl(T(Q,w)\cap T(C,w)\bigr)=1.
		\end{split}
		\]
		Therefore, $w$ is $(Q[4],C)$-extreme, and $z\in\partial L$ satisfies
		$h_K(z)=1$. Thus, by homogeneity we obtain
		\[
		g(\widetilde w)
		=h_K(\alpha x)+h_K(\beta y)-h_K(z)
		=\alpha+\beta-1>0.
		\]
		This contradicts \eqref{eq:support-theorem},
		\eqref{eq:mixed-area-deficit}, and equality in
		\eqref{eq:six-dimensional-monotonicity}.
		
		
		Suppose now that \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent. Since each ray emanating from the origin meets \(\partial L\) in exactly one point, two distinct points of \(\partial L\) cannot be positive multiples of one another. Hence, $y=-\lambda x$ for some
		$\lambda>0$. Let $\widetilde w=(x,-x)$.  Then,
		
		\[
		T(Q,\widetilde w)=\mathbb R_+x\times\mathbb R_+(-x),
		\qquad
		T(C,\widetilde w)=\ker s,
		\]
		and
		\[
		T(Q,\widetilde w)\cap T(C,\widetilde w)
		=\mathbb R_+(x,-x)
		\]
		which is one-dimensional. Therefore, \(\widetilde w\) determines a \((Q[4],C)\)-extreme direction after normalization. On the other hand,
		\[
		g(x,-x)=h_K(x)+h_K(-x)>0,
		\]
		yielding the same contradiction. This proves the forward implication.
		
		Conversely, assume that every pair of extreme points of \(L\) lies in a common proper exposed face, and let \(w=(p,q)\in\mathbb S^5\) be \((Q[4],C)\)-extreme. If \(p=0\) or \(q=0\), then \(g(p,q)=0\). We may therefore assume that \(p,q\neq0\). The first condition in \eqref{eq:extreme-three-conditions}, together with the product formula for \(T(Q,w)\), yields
		\[
		\dim\tau(p)+\dim\tau(q)
		=\dim T(Q,w)\leq2.
		\]
		Since \(p,q\neq0\), both \(\tau(p)\) and \(\tau(q)\) have dimension at least one. The preceding inequality therefore implies
		\[
		\dim\tau(p)=\dim\tau(q)=1.
		\]
		By polar duality,
		\[
		\frac{p}{h_K(p)}
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\frac{q}{h_K(q)}
		\]
		are extreme points of \(L\). Choose \(\xi\) to expose a common proper face of \(L\) containing these points, and scale \(\xi\) so that \(h_L(\xi)=1\). It follows that
		\[
		\xi\in F(K,p)\cap F(K,q).
		\]
	Therefore,
		\[
		h_K(p+q)\geq\langle\xi,p+q\rangle
		=h_K(p)+h_K(q).
		\]
		The reverse inequality follows from the subadditivity of \(h_K\). Thus,
		\[
		g(p,q)=h_K(p)+h_K(q)-h_K(p+q)=0
		\]
		for every \((Q[4],C)\)-extreme direction. By continuity, $g$ vanishes on its closure in
		\eqref{eq:support-theorem}. Equations \eqref{eq:mixed-area-deficit} and \eqref{eq:c-mixed-volume-deficit} now give \(c=9v^2\).

label: prop:polar-classification
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By translation invariance, we may assume that \(0\in\operatorname{int}K\) and let \(L=K^\circ\). It follows from 	\eqref{eq:both-equalities} and Proposition
		\ref{prop:c-equality-facial} that every pair of extreme points of \(L\) is contained in a common proper exposed face. Let \(E\subset\operatorname{ext}L\) be finite with \(\dim\operatorname{conv}E=3\), and define
		\[
		P_E=\operatorname{conv}E.
		\]
		Every point of \(E\) is a vertex of \(P_E\). Given \(x,y\in E\), choose a proper exposed face \(F\) of \(L\) containing both points. Then \(F\cap P_E\) is an exposed face of \(P_E\) containing \(x\) and \(y\). Since every proper face of \(L\) has dimension at most two, this face is proper. Thus, \(x\) and \(y\) lie in a common facet of \(P_E\). Hence, \(P_E\) is weakly neighborly. By the classification theorem, it is combinatorially equivalent to either a pyramid or a triangular prism.
		
		
	If \(\operatorname{ext}L\) is finite, then \(L\) is a polytope. Since \(L\) is weakly neighborly, the classification theorem shows that \(L\) is either a pyramid or a triangular prism. We therefore assume that \(\operatorname{ext}L\) is infinite. Choose a seven-element subset \(E_0\subset\operatorname{ext}L\) such that
	\[
	\dim\operatorname{conv}E_0=3.
	\]
	Since every point of \(E_0\) is a vertex of \(P_{E_0}=\operatorname{conv}E_0\), the polytope \(P_{E_0}\) has seven vertices. It cannot be a triangular prism, which has only six vertices, and must therefore be a pyramid over a hexagon. Denote its unique apex by \(a\), and let \(H\) be the plane containing the other six vertices.
	
		For any \(x\in\operatorname{ext}L\setminus E_0\), define
		\(
		P_x=\operatorname{conv}(E_0\cup{x}).
		\)
		Since all eight points are extreme points of \(L\), they are vertices of \(P_x\). Moreover, \(P_x\) is weakly neighborly. As a triangular prism has only six vertices, the classification theorem implies that \(P_x\) is a pyramid. Let \(H_x\) denote its base plane, which contains seven of its eight vertices.
		
		We claim that \(H_x=H\). Otherwise, \(H_x\cap H\) would be a line and could contain at most two of the six base vertices of \(P_{E_0}\), since no three distinct extreme points of \(L\) are collinear. The only remaining vertices are \(a\) and \(x\), so \(H_x\) could contain at most four vertices, contradicting the fact that it contains seven. Hence \(H_x=H\). Since \(a\notin H\), it follows that \(x\in H\).
		
		
		
		
		Let $B=L\cap H$.  Since $\operatorname{ext} L\subset B\cup\{a\}$, the
		finite-dimensional Krein--Milman theorem gives
		\[
		L=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{ext} L)
		\subset\operatorname{conv}(B\cup\{a\})\subset L.
		\]
		Here, $B$ is compact. Thus, $\operatorname{conv}(B\cup\{a\})$ is closed and both inclusions
		are equalities.
		Moreover, $B$ is a two-dimensional compact convex body in $H$. Hence, $L$ is a
		generalized pyramid.  We have shown that $L$ is either a generalized pyramid
		or a triangular prism.
		
		Polarity preserves generalized pyramids.  Indeed, after a linear
		normalization we may write
		\[
		L=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((B\times\{-1\})\cup\{(0,t)\}\bigr),
		\qquad 0\in\operatorname{int}B\subset\mathbb{R}^2,\quad t>0.
		\]
		For $(y,s)\in\mathbb{R}^2\times\mathbb{R}$, the polar inequalities are
		\[
		h_B(y)-s\leq1,\qquad ts\leq1.
		\]
	Hence,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:polar-generalized-pyramid}
			L^\circ
			=\operatorname{conv}\left(
			\{(0,-1)\}\cup
			\bigl((1+t^{-1})B^\circ\times\{t^{-1}\}\bigr)
			\right).
		\end{equation}
		Thus, $K=L^\circ$ is either a generalized pyramid or, by face-lattice
		duality, a triangular bipyramid.
		
		
		It remains to exclude the possibility that \(K\) is a triangular bipyramid. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be its apices, and let \(p_1,p_2,p_3\) be its equatorial vertices. The three facets
		\[
		\operatorname{conv}\{a,p_1,p_2\},\qquad
		\operatorname{conv}\{b,p_2,p_3\},\qquad
		\operatorname{conv}\{a,p_3,p_1\}
		\]
		have no common point. Since equality in \eqref{eq:main-inequality} implies \(b=27v^2\), Proposition \ref{prop:polytope-b-equality} implies that every three distinct facets of \(K\) to have a nonempty intersection. This contradiction excludes the case of a triangular bipyramid. Hence, \(K\) must be a generalized pyramid.

label: prop:pyramid-formula
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first consider the case in which \(B\) is a polygon (a two-dimensional polytope). By composing a horizontal translation with a volume-preserving shear, we may assume that \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\) without changing the representation in \eqref{eq:normalized-pyramid}. Let \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\) denote the vertices of \(B\) in counterclockwise order, with indices taken modulo \(m\). Define
		\[
		e_i=p_{i+1}-p_i,
		\qquad
		d_i=\det(p_i,p_{i+1})>0.
		\]
		Then
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:d-sum}
			\sum_{i=1}^m d_i=2A.
		\end{equation}
		Let $R(a,b)=(b,-a)$.  The outer area vectors of the facets of $K$ are
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:area-vectors}
			q_0=(0,0,-A),\qquad
			q_i=\frac12(hRe_i,d_i),\quad 1\leq i\leq m.
		\end{equation*}
		By Cauchy's formula, $\Pi K$ is the zonotope generated by these area
		vectors.  The zonotope volume formula gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:zonotope-discrete}
			V_3(\Pi K)
			=\sum_{0\leq i<j<k\leq m}
			|\det(q_i,q_j,q_k)|.
		\end{equation}
		Since $B-B$ is a translate of the planar zonotope
		$\sum_i[0,e_i]$, whose area is the determinant sum in
		\eqref{eq:base-terms}, the sum of all terms involving \(q_0\) is
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-terms}
			\frac{Ah^2}{4}\sum_{i<j}|\det(e_i,e_j)|
			=\frac{Ah^2}{4}V_2(B-B).
		\end{equation}
		
		It remains to sum the terms involving three side facets.  Take
		\(
		w_i=2q_i=(hRe_i,d_i).
		\)
		The points $Re_i/d_i$ are the vertices of $B^\circ$ in counterclockwise order.
		Hence,
		\[
		\det(w_i,w_j,w_k)>0\ \ (i<j<k).
		\]
		Expanding the determinant in the last coordinates, the coefficient of
		$h^2d_\ell$ in the sum of these determinants is
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:C-ell}
			C_\ell=
			\sum_{\ell<j<k}\det(e_j,e_k)
			-\sum_{i<\ell<k}\det(e_i,e_k)
			+\sum_{i<j<\ell}\det(e_i,e_j).
		\end{equation*}
		To prove that $C_\ell=2A$, we define
		\[
		E_-:=\sum_{i<\ell}e_i,\qquad
		E_+:=\sum_{i>\ell}e_i,\qquad
		S:=\sum_{i<j}\det(e_i,e_j).
		\]
		Since $E_-+e_\ell+E_+=0$, we have
		\[
		\det(E_-,E_+)=-\det(E_-,e_\ell),
		\qquad
		\det(e_\ell,E_+)=\det(E_-,e_\ell).
		\]
		Decomposing \(S\) according to the positions of the indices relative to \(\ell\), and then using the preceding two identities, we obtain
		\[
		\begin{split}
			S
			&=\sum_{i<j<\ell}\det(e_i,e_j)
			+\sum_{\ell<i<j}\det(e_i,e_j)
			-\det(E_-,E_+)\\
			&=C_\ell.
		\end{split}
		\]
		Finally, using \[ p_i=p_1+\sum_{j<i}e_j \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_i e_i=0, \] together with the polygonal area formula and the bilinearity of the determinant, we obtain 	\[
		2A=\sum_i\det(p_i,p_{i+1})
		=\sum_i\det(p_i,e_i)
		=\sum_{j<i}\det(e_j,e_i)=S.
		\]
		Thus, $C_\ell=2A$ for every $\ell$.  Together with
		\eqref{eq:d-sum}, this yields
		\[
		\sum_{i<j<k}\det(w_i,w_j,w_k)
		=h^2\sum_\ell C_\ell d_\ell=4A^2h^2.
		\]		
		Since $q_i=w_i/2$, the terms in \eqref{eq:zonotope-discrete} involving only side facets contribute a total of \(A^2h^2/2\). Combining this identity with \eqref{eq:base-terms} proves \eqref{eq:pyramid-projection-volume} for polygons.
	
		To extend \eqref{eq:pyramid-projection-volume} to an arbitrary planar convex body \(B\), we choose a sequence of polygons \(B_k\) converging to \(B\) in the Hausdorff metric, and let
		\[
		A_k=V_2(B_k),
		\qquad
		K_k=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((B_k\times\{0\})\cup\{(0,h)\}\bigr).
		\]
		Then \(A_k\to A\), \(K_k\to K\), \(B_k-B_k\to B-B\), and \(\Pi K_k\to\Pi K\) in the Hausdorff metric. By the continuity of volume, passing to the limit in \eqref{eq:pyramid-projection-volume} for \(K_k\) establishes the same formula for \(K\). Since
		\[
		V_3(K)=\frac{Ah}{3},
		\]
		substituting this into \eqref{eq:pyramid-projection-volume} yields \eqref{eq:pyramid-ratio}.

label: eq:PiQ-cube
title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\) be the standard basis of \(\mathbb R^m\), and define
	\[
	q_i=P_Fe_i\in F,
	\qquad 1\le i\le m.
	\]
	Since \(P_F\) maps \(\mathbb R^m\) onto \(F\), the vectors \(q_1,\ldots,q_m\) span \(F\). Moreover, it follows from \(F\subset\mathbf 1^\perp\) that
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^{m} q_i
	=
	P_F\mathbf{1}
	=
	0.
	\]
	Suppose that \(v\in F\) satisfies
	\[
	\langle v,q_i\rangle\ge 0
	\ \ \text{for every }i.
	\]
	Taking the inner product of \(v\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m q_i=0\) shows that
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^m\langle v,q_i\rangle=0.
	\]
	Hence \(\langle v,q_i\rangle=0\) for every \(i\). Since the \(q_i\) span \(F\), it follows that \(v=0\).
	After we remove the zero vectors and combining positively parallel vectors by addition, Minkowski’s existence theorem \cite{Schneider2014} yields a full-dimensional polytope \(Q\subset F\) whose facet-area vectors are the corresponding vectors \(-q_i\). Cauchy’s projection formula then gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:PiQ-cube}
			\Pi Q
			=\sum_{i=1}^m[-\tfrac12q_i,\tfrac12q_i]
			=P_FC_m.
		\end{equation}
		
		Translate the section \(S\) by \(-\lambda\). That is,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-shifted-section}
			\widetilde S=S-\lambda
			=\{z\in F:z_i\geq-\lambda_i\text{ for every }i\}.
		\end{equation}
		Since $z\in F$, we have
		\(
		\langle q_i,z\rangle=z_i
		\). Hence,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:support-shifted-section}
			h_{\widetilde S}(-q_i)\leq\lambda_i.
		\end{equation}
		By the mixed-volume integral representation we yield
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed-at-most}
			V_F(Q[n-1],\widetilde S)
			=\frac1n\sum_{q_i\ne0}
			\lVert q_i\rVert h_{\widetilde S}\!\left(-\frac{q_i}{\lVert q_i\rVert}\right)
			=\frac1n\sum_{q_i\ne0}h_{\widetilde S}(-q_i)
			\leq\frac1n\sum_i\lambda_i=\frac1n.
		\end{equation}
  Since every
		$\lambda_i>0$, the origin lies in $\operatorname{relint}\widetilde{S}$.
		Thus, $\widetilde S$ is an $n$-dimensional convex body in $F$.
		It follows from Minkowski's first inequality that
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:minkowski-first-transfer}
			V_F(Q)^{n-1}V_F(\widetilde S)
			\leq V_F(Q[n-1],\widetilde S)^n\leq n^{-n}.
		\end{equation}
		Since $V_F(\widetilde S)=V_F(S)$, 
		equations \eqref{eq:PiQ-cube}-\eqref{eq:minkowski-first-transfer} imply that
		\[
		\frac{V_F(\Pi Q)}{V_F(Q)^{n-1}}
		\geq n^nV_F(S)V_F(P_FC_m),
		\]
		which is \eqref{eq:transfer-lower}.  The last assertion follows immediately.

label: prop:codim-one-product
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:intrinsic-simplex-volume
title: Proof
body_md:
The intrinsic $(m-1)$-volume of the standard simplex is
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:intrinsic-simplex-volume}
			\mathcal H^{m-1}(\Delta_{m-1})=\frac{\sqrt m}{(m-1)!}.
		\end{equation*}
		The gradient of $s\mapsto\langle a,s\rangle$ on the affine hull of the
		simplex has norm $\lVert a\rVert$.  The coarea formula and the definition of
		$f_a$ therefore give
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:section-coarea}
			V_{F_a}\bigl((\lambda+F_a)\cap\Delta_{m-1}\bigr)
			=\frac{\sqrt m\,\lVert a\rVert}{(m-1)!}f_a(t).
		\end{equation}
		
		We next compute the cube projection.  Choose an $m\times(m-2)$ matrix
		$U$ whose columns form an orthonormal basis of $F_a$.  The zonotope
		determinant
		formula \cite{McMullen1984} gives
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:zonotope-minors}
			V_{F_a}(P_{F_a}C_m)
			=\sum_{|I|=m-2}|\det U_I|.
		\end{equation}
		Adding the two orthonormal vectors
		\(m^{-1/2}\mathbf{1}\) and \(\lVert a\rVert^{-1}a\)
		as columns to \(U\) produces an orthogonal matrix. For any index set \(I\) whose complement is \(I^c=\{i,j\}\), the complementary-minor identity for orthogonal matrices yields
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:complementary-minor}
			|\det  U_I|
			=\frac{|a_i-a_j|}{\sqrt m\,\lVert a\rVert}.
		\end{equation}
		Summing \eqref{eq:complementary-minor} in
		\eqref{eq:zonotope-minors}, we obtain
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:cube-projection-D}
			V_{F_a}(P_{F_a}C_m)
			=\frac{D(a)}{\sqrt m\,\lVert a\rVert}.
		\end{equation}
		Multiplication of \eqref{eq:section-coarea} and
		\eqref{eq:cube-projection-D} proves \eqref{eq:codim-one-product}.
		
		Since $n=m-2$, we get
		\[
		\frac{n+1}{n!}
		=\frac{m-1}{(m-2)!}
		=\frac{(m-1)^2}{(m-1)!},
		\]
		which proves the last assertion,

label: lem:cavalieri-section
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a point of \(\Delta_{10}\), let \(w\) denote the sum of its nine
		middle barycentric coordinates. When \(w>0\), write these coordinates
		as \(wp\), where \(p\in\Delta_8\). The two outer coordinates, whose sum
		is \(1-w\), can then be parametrized as
		\[
		\frac{1-w}{2}(1-v)
		\ \ \text{and}\ \ 
		\frac{1-w}{2}(1+v),
		\ \ -1\le v\le 1.
		\]
		Note that the degenerate boundary cases \(w=0\) and \(w=1\) have measure zero and
		do not affect the subsequent integration. The normalized simplex volume element is
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:cavalieri-volume-element}
			90w^8(1-w)\,dw\,d\bar p\,\frac{dv}{2}.
		\end{equation*}
		Indeed, because \(\Delta_8\) has dimension \(8\), scaling the middle simplex by \(w\) contributes the factor
		\(w^8\), while the outer
		one-dimensional simplex contributes the factor \(1-w\). The constant
		\(90\) is determined by
		\[
		\int_0^1 w^8(1-w)\,dw=\frac{1}{90},
		\]
		and \(dv/2\) is the normalized uniform measure on the interval
		\([-1,1]\).
		On the other hand,
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:cavalieri-height}
			\langle a_\varepsilon,u\rangle
			=(1-w)v+\varepsilon wL(p).
		\end{equation*}
		For fixed $p$ and $w$, the corresponding central slice is nonempty when
		\[
			w\leq\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon|L(p)|}.
		\]
		Its one-dimensional coarea factor is $[2(1-w)]^{-1}$.  Cavalieri's
		principle therefore gives
		\[
			f_{a_\varepsilon}(0)
			=45\int_{\Delta_8}\int_0^{(1+\varepsilon|L(p)|)^{-1}}
			w^8\,dw\,d\bar p
			=5I(\varepsilon).
		\]
		At $\varepsilon=0$ we have $D(a_0)f_{a_0}(0)=100$.  Proposition
		\ref{prop:codim-one-product} now yields
		\eqref{eq:base-geometric-ratio}.

label: lem:cube-folding
title: Lemma

label: eq:quantile-folding
title: Proof
body_md:
On the four-cube $C_4=[-1/2,1/2]^4$, take
		\[
			T(x)=x_1+\cdots+x_4,
		\]
		and let $q$ be the nondecreasing rearrangement of $T$ on the unit interval.
		Central reflection in the second factor of $C=C_4\times C_4$ shows that
		$T(x)+T(y)$ and $T(x)-T(y)$ have the same distribution.  Using equimeasurability and decomposing the unit square into the
		two regions \(s\ge t\) and \(s\le t\), we obtain
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantile-folding}
			\int_{C_4\times C_4}|T(x)+T(y)|\,dx\,dy
			=\int_0^1\!\int_0^1|q(s)-q(t)|\,ds\,dt
			=2\int_0^1(2s-1)q(s)\,ds.
		\end{equation}
		By symmetry under coordinate reflections, all cross terms in the
		expansion of \(T(x)^2\) integrate to zero. Hence,
		\[
			\int_0^1q(s)^2\,ds
			=\int_{C_4}T(x)^2\,dx
			=4\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}r^2\,dr
			=\int_0^1(2s-1)^2\,ds.
		\]
		Applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to \eqref{eq:quantile-folding} and using the
		equality of the second moments above, it follows that
		\[
			\begin{split}
			\int_{C_4\times C_4}|T(x)+T(y)|\,dx\,dy
			&\leq2\int_0^1q(s)^2\,ds\\
			&=\int_{C_4\times C_4}(T(x)+T(y))^2\,dx\,dy.
			\end{split}
		\]
		We claim that the first inequality above is strict. Equality in the
		Cauchy--Schwarz inequality would imply that \(q(s)\) is proportional
		to \(2s-1\) almost everywhere. Since \(q\) is the quantile function of
		\(T\), this would force \(T\) to be uniformly distributed on an
		interval. This conclusion is incompatible with the geometry of the upper level sets of \(T\) near its
		maximum value \(2\). For every sufficiently small \(\delta>0\), the
		set
		\[
		T^{-1}\bigl((2-\delta,2]\bigr)
		\]
		is a vertex cap of \(C_4\) and is homothetic to a fixed four-dimensional simplex with homothety ratio
		\(\delta\). Its volume is therefore
		proportional to \(\delta^4\). By contrast, a uniformly distributed random variable would assign mass of order \(\delta\) to the interval \((2-\delta,2]\). Hence equality cannot occur, and the first inequality
		is strict. Since \(T(x)+T(y)\) is the diagonal coordinate \(h\) on
		\(C\), this proves \eqref{eq:cube-folding}.

label: prop:nine-section
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Introduce ordered variables
		\[
		0\le x_1\le\cdots\le x_8\le 1
		\]
		and parametrize \(p=(p_{-4},\ldots,p_4)\in\Delta_8\) by the successive
		gaps between these variables
		\[
		(p_{-4},\ldots,p_4)
		=
		\bigl(x_1,x_2-x_1,\ldots,x_8-x_7,1-x_8\bigr).
		\]
		In affine coordinates, this change of variables has Jacobian determinant one, and a straightforward telescoping calculation yields
	\begin{equation*}
			L(p)=4-\sum_{i=1}^8x_i.
		\end{equation*}
		Let
		\[
		\mathcal O
		=
		\bigl\{x\in[0,1]^8:0\le x_1\le\cdots\le x_8\le1\bigr\}.
		\]
		Under the gap parametrization above, the normalized volume measure
		\(d\bar p\) on \(\Delta_8\) pulls back to \(8!\,dx\) on \(\mathcal O\).
		Up to a set of measure zero, the cube \([0,1]^8\) is the disjoint union
		of the \(8!\) coordinate permutations of \(\mathcal O\). Since the functions
		\[
		x\longmapsto
		\left|4-\sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i\right|
		\ \ \text{and} \ \
		x\longmapsto
		\left(4-\sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i\right)^2
		\] are invariant under coordinate permutations, it follows that
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\int_{\Delta_8}|L(p)|\,d\bar p
		=
		\int_{[0,1]^8}
		\left|4-\sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i\right|\,dx \ \ \text{and} \ \
		\int_{\Delta_8}L(p)^2\,d\bar p
		=
		\int_{[0,1]^8}
		\left(4-\sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i\right)^2\,dx.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Under the translation \(z_i=x_i-\frac12\), we obtain
	\[
	4-\sum_{i=1}^{8}x_i=-\sum_{i=1}^{8}z_i.
	\]
Hence, it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cube-folding} that 
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:folded-simplex}
		\int_{\Delta_8}|L|\,d\bar p
		<\int_{\Delta_8}L^2\,d\bar p.
	\end{equation}
	
	For \(0<\varepsilon<\frac14\), the nine middle coordinates
	\(\varepsilon j\), \(-4\le j\le4\), lie strictly between the two outer
	coordinates \(-1\) and \(1\). For each middle coordinate, the sum of its
	distances to the two outer coordinates is
	\[
	(1+\varepsilon j)+(1-\varepsilon j)=2.
	\]
	Thus, the contributions involving at least one outer coordinate remain
	unchanged, and only the pairwise distances among the middle coordinates
	depend on \(\varepsilon\). Therefore,
	\[
	D(a_\varepsilon)=D(a_0)+\varepsilon D(b).
	\]
	Since the coordinates of \(b=(j)_{j=-4}^{4}\) are ordered, it follows that
	\[
	D(b)
	=
	\sum_{-4\le i<j\le4}(j-i)
	=
	2\sum_{j=-4}^{4}j^2.
	\]
For normalized volume on the standard simplex, we have
		\[
			\int_{\Delta_8}p_i^2\,d\bar p=\frac{2}{9\cdot10},
			\qquad
			\int_{\Delta_8}p_ip_k\,d\bar p=\frac{1}{9\cdot10}
			\quad(i\neq k).
		\]
		Using the standard second-moment formula for normalized volume on
		\(\Delta_8\), together with
		\[
		\sum_{j=-4}^{4}j=0,
		\]
		we obtain, upon expanding \(L^2\),
		\[
		\int_{\Delta_8}L(p)^2\,d\bar p
		=
		\left(\sum_{j=-4}^{4}j^2\right)
		\mathbin{\Big/}
		(9\cdot10).
		\]			
		Since $D(a_0)=20$, this is equivalent to
		$D(b)/D(a_0)=9\int_{\Delta_8}L^2\,d\bar p$.
		Moreover, differentiation under the integral sign gives
		\[
			I'(0+)=-9\int_{\Delta_8}|L|\,d\bar p.
		\]
		Differentiating \eqref{eq:base-geometric-ratio} from the right at \(\varepsilon=0\), and using
		\(I(0)=1\), we therefore conclude that
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:positive-first-variation}
			\begin{aligned}
				\Gamma_0'(0+)
				&=
				\frac{D(b)}{D(a_0)}+I'(0+)\\
				&=
				9\int_{\Delta_8}
				\bigl(L(p)^2-|L(p)|\bigr)\,d\bar p
				>0,
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation*}
		where the strict inequality follows from \eqref{eq:folded-simplex}.  Since
		$\Gamma_0(0)=1$, the desired strict inequality holds for every sufficiently
		small positive $\varepsilon$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix \(n\geq 9\) and let \(r=n-9\). Applying Proposition \ref{prop:transfer} to the data defined in \eqref{eq:lifted-data}, we obtain a full-dimensional polytope
		\[
		Q_n\subset F_r\cong\mathbb{R}^n
		\]
		with at most \(m_r=n+2\) facets. Combining the estimate in Proposition \ref{prop:transfer} with Proposition \ref{prop:all-sections}, we have
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\mathcal{P}_n(Q_n)
			&\geq
			n^n
			V_{F_r}\bigl((\lambda^{(r)}+F_r)\cap\Delta_{n+1}\bigr)
			V_{F_r}\bigl(P_{F_r}C_{n+2}\bigr) \\
			&>
			\frac{(n+1)n^n}{n!}.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Thus, \(Q_n\) satisfies \eqref{eq:main-lower}, completing the proof.
